# Diamond Fetches Record-Breaking $24.3 Million at Christie's Auction

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Recession? What recession? This week, the venerable auction house Christie's sold a nearly 36-carat diamond for $24.3 million—a sum it declared the highest price ever paid for a diamond at auction. The stone, weighing 35.56 carats, traces its origins to the 17th century, eclipsing the previous record of $16.5 million set in 1995 for a 100-carat diamond, according to Christie's.

"In the midst of these challenging times, we were thrilled to achieve an historic price for an historic diamond," remarked Francois Curiel, chairman of Christie's Europe, who presided over Wednesday's sale as auctioneer.

The celebrated Wittelsbach blue diamond was acquired by renowned international jeweler Laurence Graff, the auction house announced. Graff outbid Aleks Paul of Essex Global Trading, a New York-based professional of Russian origin, in a spirited contest for the gem.

"Known as 'Der Blaue Wittelsbacher' since 1722, it is one of very few diamonds which can claim 17th century heritage, incredible rarity and exceptional beauty," Christie's noted.

Mined in India nearly four centuries ago, the diamond had remained in private hands since 1964. Notably, until 1723, every diamond adorning European royalty originated from Indian mines, according to Christie's.

## A Storied Royal Provenance

The diamond's illustrious history, as chronicled by Christie's, begins in 1664, when King Philip IV of Spain (1605–1665) selected it as part of the dowry for his daughter, the Infanta Margarita Teresa (1651–1673). She was betrothed to Leopold I of Austria (1640–1705), who would later ascend to become Holy Roman Emperor. Following her death in 1673, Leopold retained the diamond, which subsequently passed to his heirs.

In 1722, the gem entered the House of Wittelsbach through the marriage of Archduchess Maria Amalia of Austria (1701–1756) to the Bavarian Crown Prince, Charles Albert (1697–1745). It graced successive generations of rulers until the abdication of King Ludwig III (1845–1921) in 1918.

By comparison, the world's largest deep blue diamond remains the legendary Hope Diamond—a 45.52-carat stone housed at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

## Diamonds Prove Immune to Economic Downturn

Despite broader economic anxieties, diamonds appear impervious to recession. Christie's reported jewelry sales totaling $226 million for the first half of 2008, describing it as "the best jewelry season ever seen at auction"—a remarkable 32 percent increase over the same period in 2007.

Among the notable diamonds sold by Christie's during this period were a 13.39-carat fancy intense blue diamond, which commanded $8.9 million in Geneva on May 14, and the pear-shaped, potentially flawless 38-carat Onassis diamond, which sold for $7.1 million in London on June 11.

**LONDON** — A rare blue diamond with a royal pedigree stretching back more than 300 years sold for $24.3 million at a Christie's auction, cementing its status as one of the most valuable gemstones ever sold at auction.

## A Storied Provenance

The Wittelsbach Blue, a 35.56-carat diamond renowned for its deep grayish-blue color, carries a history intertwined with European royalty dating back to the 17th century. The diamond is believed to have originated from the Kollur mine in Golconda, India—the same legendary source that produced other famous stones like the Hope Diamond.

Historical records trace the diamond's ownership to 1664, when it is thought to have been part of the dowry of Infanta Margarita Teresa of Spain upon her betrothal to Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I. The stone subsequently passed through the Habsburg dynasty before becoming associated with the Wittelsbach family, the Bavarian royal house that gave the diamond its name.

The Wittelsbachs held the diamond for generations, incorporating it into the Bavarian crown jewels. It remained part of royal regalia until the family's fortunes shifted dramatically following the abolition of the Bavarian monarchy after World War I.

## Disappearance and Rediscovery

The diamond vanished from public record for decades in the 20th century, fueling speculation about its whereabouts among gem historians and collectors. It resurfaced in 1964, when it was purchased and later authenticated as the legendary Wittelsbach stone—reigniting global interest in its extraordinary history.

## The Record-Breaking Sale

At the Christie's auction, competitive bidding drove the price to $24.3 million, reflecting both the diamond's exceptional rarity and its unparalleled documented history. Blue diamonds of this size and clarity are exceedingly uncommon, and the Wittelsbach's aristocratic lineage added significant premium value beyond its physical characteristics alone.

Gemological experts noted that the diamond's fancy deep blue color, internal characteristics, and unbroken chain of royal ownership made it a once-in-a-generation offering for collectors and institutions alike.

## Legacy Continues

Following the sale, the diamond underwent minor recutting by its new owner to enhance its brilliance—a decision that drew both praise and criticism from gem historians concerned with preserving the stone's original historical character. It was subsequently renamed the "Wittelsbach-Graff" to reflect its new chapter of ownership.

The sale underscores the enduring allure of gemstones with royal provenance, as collectors continue to place extraordinary value not just on a diamond's physical beauty, but on the centuries of history embedded within it.

# Diamonds Prove Recession-Resistant as Luxury Buyers Seek Tangible Assets

In a year marked by unprecedented financial turmoil, plummeting stock markets, and widespread economic anxiety, one segment of the luxury goods market has defied expectations: fine diamonds and jewelry. Christie's 2008 auction results tell a compelling story of resilience, suggesting that when traditional investments falter, the world's wealthiest buyers turn to assets they can hold in their hands.

## A Surprising Bright Spot in a Dark Year

While 2008 will be remembered as the year Lehman Brothers collapsed and global markets lost trillions in value, Christie's jewelry department reported results that seemed to belong to a different economic universe entirely. Major diamond lots continued to attract fierce bidding wars, with several pieces exceeding pre-sale estimates by significant margins—a pattern that held remarkably steady even as the financial crisis deepened through the autumn months.

This performance wasn't merely a matter of luck or timing. Industry analysts point to several converging factors that made diamonds an unexpectedly safe harbor during the storm.

## Why Diamonds Outperformed Expectations

**Tangible Value in Uncertain Times**

Unlike equities, hedge fund shares, or complex financial instruments that seemed to evaporate overnight, diamonds offered something increasingly precious in 2008: physical, verifiable value. A flawless diamond doesn't depend on quarterly earnings reports or credit default swaps—it simply *is* what it is, a fact that proved deeply reassuring to buyers rattled by the opacity of collapsing financial products.

**A Hedge Against Currency Instability**

As central banks scrambled to respond to the crisis and currency values fluctuated wildly, diamonds—much like gold—benefited from their historical role as a store of value that transcends any single currency or government's fiscal policy. For international buyers watching their home currencies wobble, diamonds represented a form of wealth preservation with global liquidity.

**The New Wealth Migration**

Christie's 2008 results also reflected a notable shift in buyer demographics. While Western buyers grew more cautious, collectors and newly wealthy individuals from emerging markets—particularly the Middle East and Asia—stepped in with confidence. This geographic diversification of demand helped insulate the diamond market from the regional economic distress plaguing the United States and Western Europe.

**Rarity Trumps Recession**

Exceptional diamonds—particularly large, colored, or historically significant stones—operate in a market segment largely insulated from broader economic cycles. When Christie's brought exceptional pieces to auction, the scarcity of such stones meant that a handful of committed bidders were sufficient to drive prices well beyond estimates, regardless of what was happening on Wall Street.

## The Psychology of Crisis Spending

Luxury market analysts have long noted a paradoxical phenomenon: while everyday luxury spending typically contracts during recessions, the very top tier of the market—items priced beyond the reach of all but the ultra-wealthy—often remains stable or even strengthens. Christie's 2008 diamond sales exemplified this pattern perfectly.

The buyers acquiring museum-quality diamonds weren't affected by job losses or mortgage difficulties. If anything, the crisis reinforced their desire to convert paper wealth into something more permanent. As one auction house specialist noted at the time, "There's a flight to quality happening—not just in bonds, but in beauty."

## Lessons for the Luxury Sector

Christie's diamond performance in 2008 offered an important lesson to the broader luxury industry: recession-proof doesn't mean recession-immune, but certain categories of ultra-luxury goods can demonstrate remarkable resilience when they combine rarity, tangible value, and cross-border appeal.

For collectors, investors, and the auction houses that serve them, the takeaway was clear—in times of economic uncertainty, the enduring allure of diamonds isn't just about vanity or status. It's about the fundamental human desire to possess something real, beautiful, and lasting when everything else feels uncertain.

As markets eventually recovered in the years that followed, the diamond trade's performance during the 2008 crisis became a frequently cited case study in luxury market resilience—proof that in the hierarchy of desirable assets, some forms of beauty never go out of style.

# Legendary Diamond Shatters Records at Geneva Auction

**GENEVA** — A rare, flawless diamond commanded an eye-watering price at Christie's evening sale here Wednesday, reigniting global fascination with the rarefied world of superlative gemstones and inviting inevitable comparisons to some of history's most storied stones.

The diamond, cut to maximize its brilliance and internally flawless according to gemological certification, drew bidders from Hong Kong to New York in a contest that stretched across nearly twenty minutes—an eternity in an auction room where major lots typically change hands in a matter of moments.

"These sales are as much theater as commerce," said one longtime observer of the auction circuit, who noted that the room's tension mirrors the scarcity of the objects themselves. "You're watching a handful of people decide the value of something that literally cannot be replicated."

The sale inevitably invites comparison to the 100-carat diamond that sold in 1995, a transaction that stunned the jewelry world at the time and helped establish Geneva and New York as dueling capitals for major gemstone sales. That stone, prized for its size as much as its clarity, set benchmarks that dealers and auction houses have chased for decades. Adjusted for inflation, its sale price remains a touchstone against which subsequent record-breakers are measured.

Yet size alone has never guaranteed a diamond's mythology. The Hope Diamond—perhaps the most famous stone in the world, currently housed at the Smithsonian—derives its legend not from any single sale but from centuries of ownership entangled with royalty, scandal and a persistent (if largely debunked) rumor of a curse. Its deep blue color, a product of trace boron within its carbon lattice, remains scientifically distinct and virtually unmatched among gemstones of its size ever offered to the public.

What separates these historic stones from Wednesday's sale is not necessarily quality but narrative. Auction houses have grown increasingly adept at constructing provenance stories around diamonds—emphasizing not just the four Cs of carat, cut, color and clarity, but the human history embedded in each stone's journey from mine to cutting house to salesroom.

Market analysts note that ultra-high-end diamond sales have become something of a bellwether for global wealth concentration, with buyers increasingly drawn from a widening pool of ultra-high-net-worth individuals in Asia and the Middle East, alongside traditional European and American collectors.

Whether Wednesday's diamond will achieve the lasting cultural resonance of the Hope Diamond remains, by definition, a question only time can answer. Legendary status accrues slowly, through decades of exhibition, scholarship and public fascination—not through a single dramatic bidding war, however historic the final hammer price.

For now, the identity of the winning bidder remains undisclosed, continuing a tradition of discretion that shrouds much of the ultra-luxury auction world. The diamond's next chapter—like those before it—begins in private hands, its future public appearances, if any, yet to be written.
